chief_complaint: severe abdominal bloating, diarrhea, and weight loss after eating bread
hpi_details: A 65-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe abdominal bloating, diarrhea, and weight loss after eating bread. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his digestive system has developed an intolerance to modern yeast or chemical preservatives used in commercial supermarket bread.
concerns: He is worried that losing so much weight without trying means he has an undetected stomach tumor like his father had.
expectations: He hopes to get tested for a food allergy and receive dietary guidance so he can stop the diarrhea and regain his lost weight.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Coeliac Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes ordering a tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody test and advising against starting a gluten-free diet before endoscopy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe abdominal bloating, diarrhea, and weight loss after eating bread

Key HPI features: A 65-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe abdominal bloating, diarrhea, and weight loss after eating bread. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Coeliac Disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Coeliac Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Irritable bowel syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: severe weight loss or signs of malabsorption (anaemia, osteoporosis, failure to thrive), GI bleeding or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, or persistent symptoms despite a strict gluten-free diet.
management_principles: Order tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody, advise against gluten-free diet before EGD
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of severe abdominal bloating, diarrhea, and weight loss after eating bread. HPI: gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Coeliac Disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Coeliac Disease.
reference_soap.plan: While the patient continues a gluten-containing diet, order tissue transglutaminase IgA together with total IgA; use an IgG-based test when IgA deficient. Refer for duodenal biopsy when serology or suspicion supports celiac disease, and do not start a gluten-free diet before diagnostic testing is complete.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Coeliac Disease
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Coeliac Disease
Implement evidence-based management plan: Order tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody, advise against gluten-free diet before EGD

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune reaction to gluten in wheat damages the small bowel lining, causing bloating, diarrhoea, and weight loss after eating bread and similar foods.
red_flags: Severe weight loss or signs of malabsorption (anaemia, osteoporosis, failure to thrive)
GI bleeding or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia — should also prompt evaluation for other GI pathology
Persistent symptoms despite a strict gluten-free diet — raises concern for refractory coeliac disease or enteropathy-associated lymphoma

must_ask.say: Do the symptoms get worse after eating bread, pasta, or other wheat foods?
Do you get a lot of bloating and gas?
Are your stools loose or watery, and do they smell particularly bad?
Have you lost weight without trying to?
Have you been feeling unusually tired or run down?
Does anyone in your family have coeliac disease or an autoimmune condition?

history.answer: I have been having terrible bloating, loose watery stools, and I have lost weight recently, especially after I eat bread.
It started about two months ago and has been gradually getting worse over the last few weeks.
I go to the bathroom about four to six times a day, and the stools are loose, bulky, foul-smelling, and greasy.
No, I have not noticed any red blood, dark black stools, or mucus in the toilet.
No, once I go to sleep, the diarrhea does not wake me up in the middle of the night.
I get crampy lower belly discomfort before using the bathroom, and having a bowel movement gives me some relief.
I have not had any fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting.
My belly gets visibly swollen, tight, and filled with gas about an hour after eating meals.
No lightheadedness, and I am drinking plenty of water and urinating normally every few hours.
I thought maybe my stomach has just become sensitive to the chemicals and yeast they use in commercial supermarket bread nowadays.
No, I have not traveled recently, gone camping, or drank untreated spring or well water.
No, I have not taken any antibiotics in the past year, nor have I stayed in a hospital.
I have lost around 5 kilograms over the past two months without trying to diet.
The bloating and loose stools flare up significantly whenever I eat bread, pasta, or bakery items made with wheat flour.
Drinking milk does not seem to trigger it the way bread and pastries do.
I do not have alternating constipation, and the episodes happen regardless of whether I feel stressed.
I have felt constantly worn out and fatigued lately, even after getting a full night of sleep.
No, I do not have joint swelling, rash, blisters, sores in my mouth, or red eyes.
No heart racing, no sensitivity to heat, and no facial flushing or sweating spells.
I thought maybe my stomach has just become sensitive to the chemicals and yeast they use in commercial supermarket bread nowadays.
I've dropped so much weight without trying that I'm terrified I might have stomach cancer like my father had in his sixties.
I'm hoping you can run an allergy test for bread ingredients and suggest something to settle my bowels so I can put weight back on.
I have never had any major medical illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney trouble.
I have never had any surgeries or previous hospital admissions.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or nutritional supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications or food.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I drink one or two glasses of beer socially on weekends, but nothing heavy.
I am a retired accountant, and I live comfortably at home with my wife.
There is no family history of colon cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or diagnosed celiac disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
No significant drop in blood pressure or increase in heart rate upon standing.
Mild conjunctival pallor without scleral icterus.
Oral mucosa is pink and moist without aphthous ulcers or glossitis.
Mild symmetrical abdominal distension without visible peristalsis, scars, or caput medusae.
Bowel sounds are slightly hyperactive and audible in all four quadrants without bruits.
Diffuse generalized tympany throughout the abdomen; no shifting dullness.
Abdomen is soft with mild diffuse non-localized discomfort on deep palpation, but no true tenderness, guarding, or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness in any quadrant.
Normal sphincter tone, no rectal masses or palpable lesions, and no blood on the examining glove.
Normal skin turgor without vesicular eruptions, pruritic papules, or signs of dermatitis herpetiformis.
No pretibial or ankle edema bilaterally.
